passage: For three years I defended the paper ledger at our family printing business. My sister Usha kept saying we should move orders to a simple spreadsheet. I kept saying paper was safer, customers liked the personal touch, computers crash. Then last December we lost two big orders because a ledger page was smudged and nobody could read the dates. Usha put the smudged page in front of me without a word. I, Vishal, stood there for a long time. It would have been easy to blame the smudge. Instead I said, 'I was wrong about the ledger. It's cost us more than I wanted to see. From January, orders go on the spreadsheet, and I'll learn it first.' It stung. But it was one sting, and we haven't lost an order since.

qa.a: They lost two big orders.

qa.q: Why did Vishal stand looking at the page for a long time?
qa.a: Vishal was caught between pride in a three-year position and clear evidence against it, and admitting the error felt like a real cost.

qa.q: What made Vishal's admission useful and not just an apology?
qa.a: Vishal named the mistake plainly and stated exactly what would change, orders on the spreadsheet from January with Vishal learning it first, so the admission led to action.

qa.q: How might Usha feel hearing 'I was wrong about the ledger'?
qa.a: Usha would likely feel relieved and respected 🙂 after three years of suggesting the change, and glad not to have to argue any more.

grounding: Shows an adult who, faced with lost orders, admits a long-defended choice was wrong and states what will change.

passage:
Supervisor's note, water-supply project, Friday
For six weeks Thomas has insisted on the pipe route he designed along the east road, even after the soil tests came back rocky. Today, after the second drill bit broke, I watched him look at the test reports for a long time. Then he came to the site office and said, in front of the whole crew, 'I was wrong about the east route. I didn't want to see it because it was my idea. We should switch to the west side, and I'll redo the drawings by Wednesday.' It took some courage. The crew relaxed at once; two of them had been worried about raising it. I told him that saying this now has probably saved us a month. I've approved the switch and asked him to lead the new survey.
Chinmay

qa.q: By when did Thomas say he would redo the drawings?
qa.a: Thomas said he'd redo the drawings by Wednesday.

qa.q: What does 'I didn't want to see it because it was my idea' show about Thomas?
qa.a: It shows Thomas had noticed his pride holding him back, and was willing to name that feeling instead of hiding behind excuses.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay ask Thomas to lead the new survey?
qa.a: It showed that admitting a mistake doesn't cost trust, and it let Thomas turn the change into fresh work of his own rather than a defeat.

qa.q: How did the crew experience Thomas's admission?
qa.a: The crew relaxed at once; two had been worried about raising it, so hearing Thomas say it himself took the pressure off them.

grounding: Shows a supervisor's note on a young engineer who admits a long-defended route was wrong, says what will change, and keeps the team's trust.

passage:
Sunday, 11 p.m.
The scooter broke down again today, on the flyover, in the rain. Fifth time since Diwali. I pushed it half a kilometre. For a year I've told everyone it was a great buy. Before I bought it, Dilnaz said the engine sounded wrong. I told her she didn't know scooters. Every time it broke, I said 'every vehicle has issues'. Tonight, soaked, I added up the repair bills. More than half of what I paid for it. So. Writing it here first because it's hard: I was wrong. I bought it because it was cheap and shiny and I wanted to prove I could decide alone. Tomorrow I'll tell Dilnaz she was right, and ask her to come with me to the mechanic to find out what it would sell for.
It stings. But less than the flyover did.
Zeenat

qa.q: How many times had the scooter broken down since Diwali?
qa.a: It was the fifth time since Diwali.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat keep saying 'every vehicle has issues'?
qa.a: Zeenat had wanted to prove an ability to decide alone, so each breakdown threatened that pride and got explained away.

qa.q: What makes Zeenat's plan for tomorrow a good one?
qa.a: Zeenat will admit it to Dilnaz directly and take a concrete step, asking the mechanic about selling, which trades a little pride for an end to the repair bills.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz respond when told she was right?
qa.a: Dilnaz will probably feel relieved and kind rather than smug, especially since Zeenat is asking for company at the mechanic.

grounding: Shows an adult who, after repeated breakdowns and adding up repair bills, admits in a diary that a long-defended purchase was a mistake and plans what to change.

passage:
The youth club in Kumarakom met on the temple verandah after the evening lamp. Joseph, the club secretary, had the attendance register open on his knees.

For three years he had insisted that the village football tournament be held in May, "the way our fathers did it." Every year Reena, the treasurer, had suggested moving it to December. Every year he'd said no.

Tonight he read out the numbers. Teams: eleven, then eight, then five. Spectators: fewer each year. Two players had fainted in the heat last May.

He closed the register. "I was wrong," he said. "Reena was right. I kept May because I didn't want to change what I'd defended. That was pride."

A few people shifted. Somebody coughed.

"So here's what changes," Joseph said. "This year, the tournament is in December. Reena, can you and I visit the other villages together next week and invite their teams back?"

Reena smiled. "Next Sunday."

qa.q: How many teams entered in the most recent year?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: How did Joseph likely feel saying "That was pride" in front of everyone?
qa.a: He probably felt a sting of embarrassment, admitting a choice he'd defended for years. The shifting and coughing show it wasn't easy for anyone.

qa.q: Why did Joseph's admission work better than quietly changing the date?
qa.a: By saying clearly he was wrong and naming the change, Joseph gave credit to Reena and a fresh start to the club. A little pride lost now can save the tournament.

qa.q: How might Reena feel after years of being told no?
qa.a: Reena may feel relieved and quietly vindicated, and pleased to work with Joseph on inviting the teams. The quick "Next Sunday" suggests Reena is ready to move on, not gloat.

grounding: A village youth club secretary sees falling numbers, admits his long-held choice of month was a mistake, and states what will change.

passage: For two years Hana had defended her choice of supplier for the café. When Chen, her business partner, complained about late deliveries, she'd said they were the only ones with organic flour at that price, and that he was being impatient. This month she finally sat down with the delivery log herself. Eleven late deliveries in eight weeks. Two sacks of flour with weevils she'd put down to bad luck. Four mornings they'd opened without croissants. She read it twice, then went to find Chen, who was wiping down the counter. 'I was wrong about the supplier,' she said. 'I kept defending it because I'd chosen it. Here's what changes: we try the mill on Fraser Street for a month, and we check the log together every Friday.' Chen put the cloth down. 'Thank you,' he said. 'That can't have been easy.' 'Easier than another year without croissants.'

qa.q: How many late deliveries were in the log over eight weeks?
qa.a: There were eleven late deliveries in eight weeks.

qa.q: Why had Hana defended the supplier for two years?
qa.a: She felt proud of her choice and uneasy about admitting it was poor, so she explained problems away as bad luck or Chen's impatience.

qa.q: What made Hana's admission useful rather than just an apology?
qa.a: She named the mistake, why she had held on, and exactly what would change: a new mill for a month and a weekly log check.

qa.q: How might Chen feel hearing 'I was wrong'?
qa.a: Chen seems relieved and respectful, thanking her and recognising that it was hard to say.

grounding: An adult faced with evidence against a supplier she defended for years admits the mistake and states exactly what will change.

passage: At the Monday staff meeting in the school library, Pranav asked for five minutes. For three years he had insisted on his rule for Class 8 science: no questions during the lesson, only at the end, to keep things orderly. When colleagues suggested otherwise, he'd said it worked. Then Uma, the school counsellor, had shown him the term's survey. Nineteen of his thirty-four students said they stopped following once they got lost and never asked at the end. Their test scores matched. Pranav had spent the weekend with that sheet. 'I was wrong about the questions rule,' he told the room, and his ears went red. 'I held onto it because it was mine. From tomorrow, students can put a hand up anytime, and I'll pause every ten minutes to check.' Uma nodded at him across the table. Someone started clapping, and Pranav waved them down, but he was smiling.

qa.q: How many of Pranav's students said they stopped following once they got lost?
qa.a: Nineteen of his thirty-four students said so.

qa.q: What do Pranav's red ears suggest as he admits the mistake?
qa.a: They suggest he felt embarrassed and a sting to his pride, but he chose to admit it anyway.

qa.q: Why was stating what would change important?
qa.a: It turned the admission into action, hands up anytime and a check every ten minutes, so the students benefit rather than only hearing an apology.

qa.q: How might the nineteen students feel about the new rule?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and more included, able to ask as soon as they get lost.

passage:
Subject: You were right about the pump design

Gurleen,
I owe you this in writing, since I argued so loudly in person.
For eighteen months I defended the single-pump design for the Nashik irrigation project. When you suggested two smaller pumps, I said I'd done the calculations and it would cost more. Honestly, I was attached to it because it was my first big design.
The field data from this season came in yesterday. The single pump failed twice in the peak weeks; your two smaller pumps would have kept the water flowing. I checked it three times, hoping to find an error. I didn't.
So: I was wrong. Here's what changes. I'll present your two-pump option to the client on Monday, with your name on it, and I'll add a review step so no design goes ahead on one person's say-so, including mine.
It stings a bit to write this. Less than it would sting next season.
Farhan

qa.q: What did the single pump do in the peak weeks?
qa.a: The single pump failed twice in the peak weeks.

qa.q: Why did Farhan check the data three times?
qa.a: Farhan felt proud of that first big design and uneasy about being wrong, so there was hope of finding an error that would save the old choice.

qa.q: What changes does Farhan commit to?
qa.a: Presenting Gurleen's two-pump option to the client on Monday with Gurleen's name on it, and adding a review step so no design rests on one person's say-so.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel reading this email?
qa.a: Gurleen would likely feel vindicated and respected, and perhaps moved that Farhan admitted the mistake in writing and gave credit.

grounding: In an email, an engineer faced with field data admits a long-defended design was a mistake and states what will change.

Francis, you asked on your show for a moment that changed me. Okay. I'm Shalini, I run a small printing business in Coimbatore, and for three years I insisted on using the same paper supplier, Mr Pillai's firm. My father had used them. I defended them in every meeting. Late deliveries? "Monsoon." Wrong shade? "Printer's fault."

Last year my designer, Kavi, showed me a spreadsheet: twelve late orders out of thirty, four lost clients. My face went hot. I wanted to argue. Then I heard myself about to say "monsoon" again.

So I said, in front of the whole team, "I was wrong. I kept Pillai's out of loyalty, not because it worked. From next month we'll test two other suppliers." It stung, saying it. For about a day. Since then, no lost clients.

I'm Tenzin, and I've worked with Chetan at the school for four years. For all that time he insisted on one thing: Class 8 homework every single night. When parents complained, he'd say, "Discipline builds character." When the counsellor raised stress, he'd list toppers who did homework daily.

Last month the school ran a survey. Chetan read it in the staff room, very slowly. Most students said they slept after midnight. His class's marks hadn't improved in three years.

I expected him to find a reason. Instead, at the next staff meeting, he stood up and said, "I was wrong about daily homework. The survey shows it. From next term my class gets three evenings a week, and one project instead." Someone clapped, awkwardly.

I don't know what it cost him inside. He went a bit red. But he looked lighter afterwards, and the Class 8 children definitely do.

qa.q: How many evenings a week of homework will Chetan's class get?
qa.a: Chetan's class will get three evenings a week.

qa.q: What might Chetan have felt reading the survey slowly?
qa.a: Chetan probably felt uncomfortable and embarrassed, seeing evidence against a choice he had defended for years.

qa.q: What made Chetan's statement a real correction?
qa.a: He named the mistake plainly, pointed to the evidence, and stated a specific change for next term.

qa.q: How might the Class 8 students feel about the change?
qa.a: They likely feel relieved and happier, with fewer late nights and a project instead.

grounding: A colleague describes a teacher who, faced with a survey, publicly admits a long-held homework rule was wrong and changes it.

passage:
Before, March: Mehak had chosen the flat in Panvel over Jatin's doubts. "The rent is lower, the view is great, the commute will be fine." For eight months she defended it. When Jatin looked tired, she said, "Everyone commutes."

During, November: Mehak timed her own commute for a week. Two hours and ten minutes each way, on average. She had missed three dinners and a friend's engagement. She looked at the numbers on her phone on the 10 p.m. train and felt a hot rush of pride and embarrassment together.

After, the next Sunday: over tea she said to Jatin, "I was wrong about Panvel. The lower rent isn't worth four hours a day. I'm sorry I kept arguing. When the lease ends in February, let's move closer to the station." Jatin blinked, then laughed with relief. "I've been waiting eight months to hear that."

qa.q: How long was Mehak's commute each way?
qa.a: Mehak's commute was two hours and ten minutes each way, on average.

qa.q: What did Mehak feel looking at the commute numbers on the train?

qa.q: What made Mehak's admission on Sunday work?
qa.a: She said plainly she was wrong, apologised for arguing, and stated a concrete change: moving closer when the lease ends.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel hearing Mehak admit it?
qa.a: Jatin felt relieved and laughed, having waited eight months to hear it.

passage: Lakshmi, beti, you ask how to say sorry to your team when you're the boss? Let your grandfather, Omkar Tata, tell you about the sugarcane. When I was twenty-five, I took over our five acres near Belagavi. My father grew jowar. I said, "Sugarcane pays more," and I planted it all. For three years I defended it. When the borewell ran low, I said it was a bad monsoon. When the neighbours said the cane was drinking the land dry, I said they were jealous. Then the well dried up completely in the fourth summer. I sat by it for a long time. That evening, in front of my father and my younger brothers, I said, "I was wrong about the sugarcane. qa.q: What choice in the story saved the land, and why?
qa.a: Saying "I was wrong" openly and stating the change, going back to jowar and millets, which protected the water.

passage: For two years Afreen had run her tuition centre in Hyderabad her own way: no homework, only games and projects. Parents had doubts, but she defended the method at every meeting. Then the half-yearly results came. Two-thirds of her Class 8 students had slipped in maths. She spread the mark sheets on the floor of the centre and sat among them. Nandini, who taught English there, found her like that. "Bad?" "Bad." Afreen didn't reach for an excuse this time. On Saturday she called a parents' meeting. "I believed games alone would be enough for maths. I was wrong. From Monday, we'll keep the games, but add twenty minutes of practice every day and a short weekly test." A father at the back folded his arms, then unfolded them. After the meeting, Nandini said, "That took guts." Afreen laughed shakily. "It took less than another bad year would have."

qa.q: How many of Afreen's Class 8 students slipped in maths?
qa.a: Two-thirds of her Class 8 students had slipped in maths.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling as she sat among the mark sheets?
qa.a: Afreen felt shaken and disappointed, facing clear evidence that the method she defended wasn't working.

qa.q: What did Afreen say that made her admission useful, not just an apology?
qa.a: She stated exactly what would change: keeping the games but adding daily practice and a weekly test.

qa.q: How might the father at the back have felt as he unfolded his arms?
qa.a: He seemed to soften, perhaps relieved and more trusting after hearing her admit the mistake openly.

grounding: A tuition teacher faces results against a long-held teaching choice, admits it was a mistake to parents and states what will change.
